results.summary: This design implements an I2C slave port that can read and write the instruction memory of a RISC-V processor. It exposes four registers: one to set the memory address, one to read the current value, one to write a new value, and one unused register. The I2C interface uses external SDA and SCL pins, with an additional reset and chip-select input, and provides open-drain control for SDA. Testing requires an external I2C master to issue the documented read and write transactions.

This design is a digital piano that generates twelve independent musical notes across eight octaves and can also play two predefined songs stored in RTTTL format. It uses a 1 MHz clock to produce square-wave audio output and drives an LED bar as a visualizer. The design requires external hardware: twelve momentary switches for the keys, four toggle switches for mode and octave selection, an LED bar, and a speaker with an amplifier. It is notable for its musical application and the inclusion of demo songs, but it has no silicon test report.

This design sorts four 2-bit input values using an odd-even sorting network and outputs the sorted values. The inputs are provided on ui_in[7:0] and the sorted results appear on uo_out[7:0], which are also mapped to 7-segment display segments. The sorting operation is pipelined through internal registers, requiring an external clock. The documentation is minimal, providing only a basic description and test instructions, with no silicon test results.

This design is a time-multiplexed NAND gate that implements a timer or counter, as suggested by the pin names and title. It uses a 10 MHz clock and provides outputs for a 7-segment display and a second counter. The documentation is essentially empty, with 'TODO' for both how it works and how to test, so the exact functionality cannot be determined. A silicon test report indicates the chip is working, but no further details are given.

This design generates audio using PWM output, as indicated by its title and pin names. It has two PWM audio outputs, labeled low and high. The documentation is a template with placeholder text, so no details about the synthesis method, testing, or external hardware are available. It is implemented in Wokwi, but no silicon test results are provided.

This design is an 8-bit processor that communicates with an external device via SPI and can animate a 7-segment display. It requires an external driver, such as an FPGA, to load program and data memory and to start execution. The processor supports displaying register contents or animations on the 7-segment display, with switches to control the display mode. The documentation is detailed, including test instructions, but no silicon test results are provided.

This design implements a pseudo-random number generator using two LFSRs (8-bit and 16-bit) and a 16-to-8 multiplexer. It produces 8-bit pseudo-random numbers that are displayed on two 7-segment displays. The design requires a 50 MHz clock, an enable signal, and an active-low reset. Testing involves connecting the clock and control signals and observing the random numbers on the displays. No silicon test results are provided.

This design classifies images of numbers from 0 to 7 using the 16 most significant pixels of an 8x8 image as input features. The classification result is displayed on a 7-segment display. The design requires a 10 MHz clock and uses 16 input pins for the features. Testing involves setting the feature inputs according to the pixel pattern of the desired number. The documentation is brief but sufficient, and no silicon test results are provided.

This design implements the Simon Says memory game, where the player must repeat a growing sequence of colors. The sequence is shown via four LEDs, each with a corresponding tone played through a speaker, and the score is displayed on a two-digit 7-segment display. The game requires external hardware: four push buttons with pull-down resistors, four LEDs, a speaker or buzzer, and optionally a two-digit 7-segment display. A silicon test report notes a minor bug where pressing a button immediately after failing skips the game over sound, which was fixed in a later version.

This design implements a USB to Serial bridge using the USB CDC protocol, allowing a computer to communicate with the chip as a virtual serial port. It uses a 48 MHz clock and connects to USB D+ and D- pins, requiring a 1.5k ohm pull-up resistor on D+ for device detection. Data received from the USB host appears on the rx output pins, and data can be transmitted by setting the tx input pins and asserting tx_valid. A silicon test report confirms both RX and TX work as expected, and the design is based on an open-source USB serial core.
